native_mcp_support.notes: No Meta model implements the MCP wire protocol itself. Llama 4 emits llama4_pythonic tool calls; Muse Glimmer emits ATEM XML tool calls; the hosted Muse Spark models expose OpenAI-compatible function calling. Meta's Muse Spark 1.1 announcement states the model 'zero-shot generalizes to new native tools, MCP servers, and custom skills' - that is a training/behaviour claim about tools sourced from MCP servers, not a request-level MCP connector. No documented `mcp` tool type or remote-MCP server parameter exists on the Meta Model API, so an MCP host still has to translate `tools/list` into function/ATEM tool definitions. Scope note: because the bridging happens in the host, every documented ceiling is aggregate (all servers + built-in tools in one request), never per MCP server.

Any skill instructions an external framework injects are ordinary input tokens.

function_calling.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from vLLM's serving-framework doc (correctly tier 4, not a vendor spec) to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification (meta-llama/llama-models, the vendor's model repo) defines the model's complete tool contract: 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', introduced by 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:' followed by a JSON array of {name, description, parameters} objects, and the model answers with pythonic calls - [func_name(param1=value1, param2=value2)], e.g. [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - with an alternative <function=function_name>{"param": "value"}</function> form. It states 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively'. Zero-shot function calling is therefore a documented capability of the released weights, not just a serving-stack feature; vLLM's `llama4_pythonic` parser exists to turn that pythonic output back into OpenAI-shaped tool_calls.

max_tools_hard.notes: NULL, and DOWNGRADED from high at the 2026-08-19 remediation, where the citation also moved off vLLM's serving-framework doc (graded tier 4 below) onto Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. tool_definition_shape.value: llama4_pythonic (Llama 4 chat-template tool syntax); OpenAI function JSON when served behind a vLLM/SGLang OpenAI-compatible endpoint
tool_definition_shape.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Definitions go in as OpenAI-style JSON function objects ({name, description, parameters}) inside the system (or user) message under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'; the model REPLIES in the pythonic form [func_name(param=value)], which is why vLLM recommends the `llama4_pythonic` tool parser for Llama 4 models. Footprint note: the input side is ordinary function JSON, so OpenAI-shaped token estimates transfer; the output side is not JSON and is cheaper per call.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from a third-party HuggingFace blog post to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification: function definitions are literally written into the system (or user) message ('All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'). They are therefore ordinary prompt tokens - re-sent and re-counted on every turn of a conversation unless a prefix cache absorbs them - and they compete with the prompt for the same window.

tool_search_deferral.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification, which places the full catalog up front - 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message' - and documents no runtime tool-search, lazy-loading or deferred-definition mechanism (no Claude ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH / defer_loading equivalent). Medium confidence: this is an absence claim over Meta's published spec, not an explicit vendor denial. Any deferral has to be implemented by the MCP host before the request, and every definition it does send is billed as input on every turn.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character-count or character-class cap on function names is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification shows names used verbatim inside the JSON definition and in the pythonic call ([get_weather(city="San Francisco")]) with no length or pattern rule, and there is no OpenAI-style 64-char pattern constraint to inherit because Meta hosts no API for these weights. Consequence for MCP: long client-namespaced tool names cost tokens rather than being rejected, and a name that is awkward inside the pythonic call format is a parser risk, not an API error.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No published per-tool schema size, property-count or nesting-depth limits. The effective limit is context-window consumption: tool JSON is serialized into the prompt and counted as input tokens.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No numeric ceiling on description length is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification includes `description` in each JSON function object with no length rule. The description is serialized into the system message and counts against the shared context window - that budget is the only ceiling.

max_request_size.notes: No vendor byte cap (open weights, no Meta API layer). Bounded by the serving config (vLLM --max-model-len / --max-num-batched-tokens) and GPU memory. max_tool_result_size.notes: Context-bound: tool results are appended to the prompt and count against max_model_len. max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No numeric ceiling on how many calls may be emitted in one turn is published. Meta's prompt-format specification says only that 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively' and shows a two-call example; the practical bound is the remaining output budget and the tool parser's ability to split the list.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model-level cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn is documented for Llama 4. Meta's own prompt-format specification defines the entire tool contract - the JSON function list in the system or user message and the pythonic [func_name(param=value)] reply - and says nothing about how many call/result cycles a turn may contain, and Meta hosts no API for these weights that could enforce one. Also searched the HuggingFace model card: it states no such number either. This is a host-layer property - the agent framework or MCP host decides when to stop looping - and what actually stops a long loop here is the context window filling with tool results.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model-layer limit and not documented anywhere by Meta. Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification - the complete published tool contract for these weights - never mentions MCP at all, and neither does the HuggingFace model card, so there is no vendor cap on connected MCP servers to record. Connected-server caps live in the host application (Claude Desktop, Cursor, an in-house agent) and Llama 4 open weights have no first-party host. What binds instead is the aggregate tool count and token footprint that all connected servers add up to inside the context window.

max_total_tools.notes: No vendor cap. Aggregate ceiling ~ (context_window - output headroom) / avg tool-definition tokens, set by the serving config. Host apps cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100). RE-GRADED 2026-08-19: this citation is vLLM's own tool-calling documentation - a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec - so it is tier 4, not tier 2. It documents no numeric ceiling on the aggregate tool count. No Meta page publishes one either; for self-hosted weights the real ceiling is the operator's serving config and the context window.

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open weights: there is no Meta API layer, so no tool count/name/size cap is enforced at the model API. Binding limits, in the order they usually bite: (1) the host app's aggregate tool budget (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100); (2) the serving stack - vLLM/SGLang max_model_len (default is often 16K, which silently truncates tool calls mid-generation - raise it), max_num_batched_tokens, KV-cache/GPU memory; (3) the hosted endpoint's own context cap (Groq serves Scout at 128K, OpenRouter at 1,310,720 - both far below Meta's documented 10M); (4) the ~30-50-tool aggregate selection cliff; (5) parser mismatch - tool calling requires --tool-call-parser llama4_pythonic and the matching chat template, and vLLM issue #46863 reports Llama-4 tool calls being left in content when a JSON parser is used instead.

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (no enforced 100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf contract). Schema fidelity depends entirely on the chat template and the tool-call parser. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19 to tier 4 (vLLM's own serving-framework documentation, not a vendor spec). For completeness: vLLM does expose a `strict` field on tool definitions ('For tool_choice="auto", setting strict: true on at least one tool opts in to structural-tag constraints'), but that is a vLLM feature, not a Llama 4 model contract - Meta publishes no OpenAI-style strict structured-function mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf enforcement) for these weights.

tool_definition_shape.value: llama4_pythonic (Llama 4 chat-template tool syntax); OpenAI function JSON behind a vLLM/SGLang OpenAI-compatible endpoint
tool_definition_shape.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Definitions go in as OpenAI-style JSON function objects ({name, description, parameters}) inside the system (or user) message under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'; the model REPLIES in the pythonic form [func_name(param=value)], which is why vLLM recommends the `llama4_pythonic` tool parser for Llama 4 models. Footprint note: the input side is ordinary function JSON, so OpenAI-shaped token estimates transfer; the output side is not JSON and is cheaper per call.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from a third-party HuggingFace blog post to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification: function definitions are literally written into the system (or user) message ('All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'). They are therefore ordinary prompt tokens - re-sent and re-counted on every turn of a conversation unless a prefix cache absorbs them - and they compete with the prompt for the same window.

tool_search_deferral.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification, which places the full catalog up front - 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message' - and documents no runtime tool-search, lazy-loading or deferred-definition mechanism (no Claude ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH / defer_loading equivalent). Medium confidence: this is an absence claim over Meta's published spec, not an explicit vendor denial. Any deferral has to be implemented by the MCP host before the request, and every definition it does send is billed as input on every turn.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character-count or character-class cap on function names is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification shows names used verbatim inside the JSON definition and in the pythonic call ([get_weather(city="San Francisco")]) with no length or pattern rule, and there is no OpenAI-style 64-char pattern constraint to inherit because Meta hosts no API for these weights. Consequence for MCP: long client-namespaced tool names cost tokens rather than being rejected, and a name that is awkward inside the pythonic call format is a parser risk, not an API error.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No published per-tool schema size, property-count or nesting-depth limits. The effective limit is context-window consumption - tool JSON is serialized into the prompt as input tokens.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No numeric ceiling on description length is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification includes `description` in each JSON function object with no length rule. The description is serialized into the system message and counts against the shared context window - that budget is the only ceiling.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No numeric ceiling on how many calls may be emitted in one turn is published. tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model-level cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn is documented for Llama 4. Meta's own prompt-format specification defines the entire tool contract - the JSON function list in the system or user message and the pythonic [func_name(param=value)] reply - and says nothing about how many call/result cycles a turn may contain, and Meta hosts no API for these weights that could enforce one. Also searched the HuggingFace model card: it states no such number either. This is a host-layer property - the agent framework or MCP host decides when to stop looping - and what actually stops a long loop here is the context window filling with tool results.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model-layer limit and not documented anywhere by Meta. Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification - the complete published tool contract for these weights - never mentions MCP at all, and neither does the HuggingFace model card, so there is no vendor cap on connected MCP servers to record. Connected-server caps live in the host application (Claude Desktop, Cursor, an in-house agent) and Llama 4 open weights have no first-party host. What binds instead is the aggregate tool count and token footprint that all connected servers add up to inside the context window.

native_mcp.notes: RE-SOURCED at the 2026-08-19 remediation. The previous citation was the meta-oss-cookbook agentic-fundamentals README, which documents the ATEM XML tool-block format and contains no MCP content at all. Correct tier-1 evidence is the model's own HuggingFace card, and it is what sets this value: the card reports an MCP-Atlas (Public) score of 75.5 (vs Gemma4-31B 54.2, Qwen3.6-27B 62.5), describes 'reliable tool use' handling 'a wide range of function calls, invoking tools with precise schemas throughout extended workflows', and under Scaffold Compatibility says 'Muse Glimmer works across OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and other agentic orchestration patterns'. That is a benchmark score on tasks whose tools come from MCP servers plus compatibility with external agent scaffolds - NOT an in-model MCP client: the card documents no MCP transport, connector or request parameter, and the model emits ATEM blocks (<atem:function_calls> / <atem:invoke> / <atem:parameter>), not MCP messages. Medium confidence because the card never explicitly denies MCP; it simply never documents one. Practical reading: this model is unusually good at MCP-sourced tool tasks, but the MCP client always lives in the host, so every ceiling is aggregate and the ATEM shape - not MCP JSON - is what the tokens are spent on.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Meta's own OSS cookbook shows multiple <atem:invoke> elements inside a single <atem:function_calls> block, and warns that stopping generation on <|eom|> instead of the correct stop set [<|eot|>, <|end_of_text|>] 'collapses' multi-tool turns - i.e. parallel calls are the intended behaviour.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric tool cap is documented, and for open weights there is no vendor API layer that could enforce one. Meta's cookbook explicitly provides 'no explicit guidance on token counting for tool definitions, maximum tool count, or schema size limits'. The limits that DO bind are all AGGREGATE across every connected server plus built-in tools: (1) the 131,072-token shared window, which tool definitions, the reasoning channel and the answer all draw from - roughly 8x tighter than Llama 4 Maverick's nominal 1M; (2) the serving stack's --max-model-len; (3) the host app's own tool budget (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100); (4) the empirical tool-selection cliff. max_tools_practical.notes: No Muse-Glimmer-specific degradation point has been published. tool_definition_shape.value: ATEM XML blocks (<atem:function_calls> / <atem:invoke> / <atem:parameter>) inside a channel-scoped chat template; OpenAI function JSON at the wire when served via vLLM with --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer
tool_definition_shape.notes: Meta's cookbook documents the format: '<atem:function_calls><atem:invoke name="get_weather"><atem:parameter name="city">Paris</atem:parameter></atem:invoke></atem:function_calls>', where scalars and strings are written as-is and lists/objects are JSON. Critically, an <atem:invoke> echoed inside a to=self reasoning block or a to=user answer is NOT a real call - the parser strips non-routed spans. Shape matters for footprint: ATEM XML framing is a different token cost from OpenAI function JSON for the same MCP tool.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Tool definitions are rendered into the prompt by the chat template and are consumed as input tokens from the 131,072-token window. Meta gives no token-accounting guidance for them, so measure with the public tokenizer.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No deferred / lazy tool-definition loading in the model, the chat template or the documented serving path. Any progressive disclosure is the agent harness's job.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No documented character or token limit on tool names. Names appear as the ATEM invoke `name` attribute; MCP clients that namespace names simply spend more input tokens rather than hitting a cap.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No published per-tool schema size, property-count or nesting-depth limits - Meta's cookbook states there is no explicit guidance on schema size limits. Note one real constraint from the vLLM enablement PR: the muse_glimmer parser sets supports_required_and_named = False, so tool_choice='required' and named tool choice are NOT supported and JSON guided decoding is deliberately not applied to tool arguments. Argument fidelity therefore rests on the model, not on constrained decoding.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No vendor cap. Descriptions are prompt text and count against the 131,072-token window.

max_request_size.notes: No vendor byte cap (open weights). Bounded by the serving config - the official vLLM recipe uses --max-model-len 131072 with --max-num-seqs 64 - and by KV-cache/GPU memory. max_tool_result_size.notes: Context-bound: tool results are appended to the prompt and count against --max-model-len. max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Multiple invokes per ATEM block are supported but no numeric ceiling is documented.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model- or serving-level cap on tool-call/result cycles; the agent harness decides when to force an answer.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model property - set by the MCP host. Meta ships no first-party MCP client for Muse Glimmer. tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open weights: no Meta API layer, so no tool count/name/size caps are enforced at the model API. Binding limits, in practice: (1) the 131,072-token aggregate window shared by tool definitions, reasoning channel and answer - much tighter than the Llama 4 pair, so tool footprint is a first-order concern again; (2) serving config - the official vLLM recipe requires vLLM 0.27.0+ and BOTH --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer AND --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer, because the model emits neither JSON tool calls nor tag-wrapped reasoning; omitting either leaves tool calls unparsed in content; (3) tool_choice='required' and named tool choice are unsupported (supports_required_and_named = False), so you cannot force a specific tool; (4) the stop set must be [<|eot|>, <|end_of_text|>] - stopping on <|eom|> collapses multi-tool turns; (5) as of 2026-08-19 the muse_glimmer parser is not yet listed in vLLM's tool_calling doc on main (enablement PR #51655 was still open), so pin a build that contains it; (6) host-app aggregate tool budgets (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

strict_function_schema.notes: The vLLM enablement PR sets supports_required_and_named = False for the muse_glimmer parser specifically to prevent JSON guided decoding being applied. skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: No native skills. Anything a framework injects (skill instructions, tool catalogues, retrieved context) is plain input tokens against the 131,072-token window, competing directly with the ATEM tool-definition block and the reasoning channel.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System-prompt tokens count as input. Muse Glimmer takes a functional directive in the system prompt - 'Reasoning strength: <low|medium|high|xhigh>' - so the system prompt is also the reasoning-budget control: raising reasoning strength spends output/context tokens that are then unavailable to tool definitions. No platform-injected overhead; the operator owns the whole prompt.

prompt_caching.notes: Serving-stack capability, not model-native, and with no billed discount (open weights). The official vLLM recipe is a standard prefix-caching-capable deployment (it reports a 26.8M-token KV pool at 4-way tensor parallelism on GB300), so a stable system-prompt + tool-definition prefix can be reused across turns. Verify prefix caching is enabled in your own build.

memory_feature.notes: No built-in persistent memory. Long-horizon state is the harness's responsibility; the model card positions the 131,072-token window plus failure recovery as the mechanism for 'long tasks'.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Open weights - no vendor price. Cost is self-hosted GPU (or CPU/NPU) compute.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: N/A - open weights, no vendor billing. Operationally, reasoning-channel tokens are generated tokens and consume the same window and the same generation time as answer tokens (see reasoning_tokens_count_as_output).

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: vLLM (official recipe): `vllm serve <model> --served-model-name muse-glimmer --tensor-parallel-size 4 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --max-model-len 131072 --max-num-seqs 64 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer --generation-config auto`. BOTH parsers are mandatory: the model emits neither JSON tool calls nor tag-wrapped reasoning, so a JSON parser leaves ATEM tool calls sitting in `content`. The parser also strips <atem:invoke> spans echoed inside to=self reasoning or to=user answers so they are not mis-executed. tool_choice='required' and named tool choice are unsupported. llama.cpp/Ollama: run the official GGUFs with --jinja so the embedded chat template frames tool calls correctly. Behind vLLM's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, MCP tool definitions serialized as OpenAI functions are translated into the ATEM block by the chat template - the model itself never sees MCP.

models.notes: NEW 2026-08-19. Muse Glimmer 30B (released 2026-08-10) is Meta's first open-weight model since Llama 4 in April 2025, the first open-weight release from Meta Superintelligence Labs, and the first Meta model under a plain Apache-2.0 licence with an UNGATED repository - a genuine break from the Llama Community License era. It is distilled from the proprietary Muse Spark family and explicitly built for agentic tool use (benchmarked on MCP-Atlas, tau3-Bench, DeepSearch QA, SWE-Bench) while fitting on a single consumer GPU (~20 GB at 4-bit). For MCP footprint work it inverts the Llama 4 story: the window is 131,072 tokens, not 1M-10M, so tool-definition footprint, tool-result size and the reasoning channel all compete for a normal-sized budget, and the ATEM XML tool shape has a different token cost than the OpenAI function JSON most footprint tooling assumes. Two operational traps: both --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer and --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer are required, and tool_choice='required'/named tool choice are not supported.
